assignment: ML-09 -- Validation and Research Claim Audit

paper_audit.finding: Finding #4 -- The Freshness Multiplier (3.2x health, 57x impressions)
paper_audit.question: paired before/after per page, or cross-sectional comparison? If cross-sectional, editor selection bias (refreshing already-promising pages) could explain most of the gap without a causal refresh effect.

paper_audit.finding: ML Appendix -- What Predicts Growth? (71% holdout accuracy, logistic regression)
paper_audit.question: was the reported 80/20 split grouped by brand, or a plain random row split? Only 57 brands in the dataset -- a random split risks brand memorization inflating holdout accuracy, per the finding below.

before_after_split_comparison.description: Same modeling frame, same Random Forest, two different splits
before_after_split_comparison.interpretation: The random split scores 20 points higher at P@50 than the honest client-holdout split on the exact same underlying data -- direct empirical evidence of memorization, and direct support for the methodology question raised against the FlyRank paper's own unstated split strategy.
before_after_split_comparison.reproducibility: identical results across 2 independent full reruns

leakage_audit.checklist_status: 8 of 9 items directly confirmed YES; population-selection item resolved as a new named limitation (see below), not a pass/fail
leakage_audit.new_limitation_found: Week 5's leakage fix (dropping rows with future-dated content_updated_date) means the modeling population is, by construction, pages NOT edited between March 15 and July. If editors preferentially refresh pages they already believe are declining, this population choice may under-represent true decliners -- a selection effect, not classic leakage, disclosed as a named limitation rather than fixed (would require point-in-time content history dim_content doesn't provide).

claim_rewrite.original: Random Forest wins at P@50 (0.64 vs 0.46) but loses at P@20 (0.60 vs 0.65).
claim_rewrite.rewritten: On this run's client-holdout test set (1,979 rows, 6 held-out clients), Random Forest was observed to score higher than Logistic Regression at Precision@50 (0.64 vs 0.46) and lower at Precision@20 (0.60 vs 0.65). This is decision-support evidence for Random Forest's precision profile at K=50 specifically, not a general claim that Random Forest is the better model.
